events.title: A stone London Bridge begins upstream
events.text: Peter de Colechurch began building the first stone London Bridge, a much earlier crossing upstream from the future Tower Bridge site.

events.title: Before the bridge: wharves, stairs and crossings
events.text: The river edge was a working port of wharves and warehouses. Irongate Stairs and nearby river stairs gave access to boats; the Tower Subway and London Bridge were established crossings before this bridge.

events.title: Stage 1: river foundations begin
events.text: Work began in April. Crews built temporary staging and began the piers and abutments; the first iron caisson was sunk in September to enclose work below the riverbed.

events.title: Stage 2: approaches and hydraulic design
events.text: The northern approach and its chain anchorage entered construction, followed by hydraulic machinery contracts. Foundation work continued in the river.

events.title: Stage 3: southern approach
events.text: The southern approach and its chain anchorage entered construction. Design work continued while crews advanced the foundations and shore structures.

events.title: Stage 4: steel and masonry superstructure
events.text: Contracts began for the iron and steel superstructure and the masonry superstructure. The contemporary contract schedule dates both awards to May.

events.title: Stage 5: foundation works and rising steelwork
events.text: Foundation and tower construction advanced from the caisson works toward the visible steel towers. The precise sequence of work during this year is not itemised in the cited contract table.
events.note: Year-specific visual state is an interpolation between the dated foundation contracts and the circa-1891 archive photograph.

events.title: Stage 6: tower frames rise
events.text: An archive photograph records both steel tower frames under construction, with the north tower further advanced and a temporary shore span carrying materials.

events.title: Stage 7: high-level walkways approach completion
events.text: The high-level walkways approached completion and the masonry work continued. Paving and lighting entered the contract programme.

events.title: Stage 8: bascule girders and finishing work
events.text: Photographs show the north bascule's four main girders and cross-bracing. Work continued toward completion of the bridge and its machinery.

events.title: Stage 9: tested and opened
events.text: The final granite stone was set in January; engineers tested the hydraulics in April. The Prince of Wales opened the bridge on 30 June.

events.title: High-level walkways close
events.text: Low use led to the closure of the elevated pedestrian routes. Many pedestrians preferred waiting at road level for the leaves to close.

events.title: Electric power replaces steam
events.text: Electric operation took over from the original steam-powered hydraulic system. The historic steam engines remain in the engine rooms.

events.title: Walkways reopen as a visitor attraction
events.text: The public could again enter the high-level walkways as part of the new visitor attraction.

facts.text: The central bascule opening is reported as 200 feet (60.96 metres) clear.
Each suspension side span is 270 feet (82.296 metres) long.
The contemporary account records about 31 million bricks and 14,000 tons of iron and steel used in construction.
The walkways allowed pedestrians to cross above the roadway while the bascules were raised; they closed to the public in 1910 and reopened in 1982.
Steam-powered bridge lifting was replaced by electric operation in 1976.

facts.title: Horses and horse-drawn traffic on Tower Bridge
facts.text: In July 1894, an estimated 8,000 horse-drawn vehicles crossed Tower Bridge each day.
facts.source_excerpt: From July, an estimated 8,000 horse-drawn vehicles and 60,000 pedestrians are crossing the Bridge daily.

facts.title: How heavy is an original bascule?
facts.text: The 1894 engineering account reports about 1,200 tons for each moving bascule leaf, including its counterbalance. This is the historical quantity as reported, not a modern metric measurement.
facts.locator: J. E. Tuit, The Tower Bridge (1894), The Hydraulic Machinery, printed p. 99

facts.title: Why is Tower Bridge painted blue?
facts.text: Tower Bridge was painted red, white and blue in 1977 to celebrate Queen Elizabeth II’s Silver Jubilee.
